slides.title: Quadratic Equations
bullets: Class 10 — NIOS Mathematics
Chapter 6
slides.speaker_notes: Welcome students. In this lesson we move from linear equations (degree 1) to quadratic equations (degree 2), develop three methods for solving them, study the discriminant, and apply quadratic equations to short word problems.

slides.title: What you'll be able to do
bullets: Recognise a quadratic equation a x^2 + b x + c = 0 and pick out a, b, c.
Solve a quadratic by factorisation.
Solve a quadratic by completing the square.
Use the quadratic (Sridharacharya) formula.
Use the discriminant to predict the nature of the roots.
Translate a short word problem into a quadratic and solve it.
slides.speaker_notes: Read each objective; ask students which they feel least sure about and weight the lesson accordingly.

slides.title: Standard form
bullets: a x^2 + b x + c = 0 with a, b, c real and a ≠ 0.
If a = 0 the x^2 term disappears and we have a linear equation.
A root is an x-value that makes the LHS zero.
Geometrically, a root is an x-intercept of y = a x^2 + b x + c.
A quadratic has at most two real roots.
slides.speaker_notes: Stress the a ≠ 0 condition and the geometric picture: a parabola can cross the axis 0, 1, or 2 times.

slides.title: Bringing equations to standard form
bullets: x + 6/x = 5 → x^2 − 5 x + 6 = 0 (multiply by x, x ≠ 0).
√(x + 4) = x − 2 → x^2 − 5 x = 0 (square both sides).
Squaring or multiplying by an unknown can introduce extraneous roots.
Always verify each candidate root in the ORIGINAL equation.
slides.speaker_notes: Highlight the danger of squaring: x = −1 in the third example formally satisfies the squared equation but not the original. Always check.

slides.title: Method 1 — Factorisation
bullets: Factor a x^2 + b x + c = (p x + q)(r x + s).
Then either p x + q = 0 or r x + s = 0 (zero-product property).
Splitting the middle term: find two numbers with product a × c and sum b.
slides.speaker_notes: Walk through the splitting step slowly on the second example: 'product −90, sum 1, so 10 and −9'.

slides.title: Method 2 — Completing the square
bullets: Key identity: x^2 + 2 p x = (x + p)^2 − p^2.
Six steps: divide by a, move constant, add (b/2a)^2, take square root, solve.
Final form: (x + b/(2a))^2 = (b^2 − 4 a c) / (4 a^2).
Carrying this out on the general equation gives the quadratic formula.
slides.speaker_notes: Long-derive once on x^2 − 6 x + 5 = 0; then point out the same six steps will produce the formula.

slides.title: Method 3 — Quadratic (Sridharacharya) formula
bullets: Works for every quadratic in standard form.
Known to Sridharacharya (9th-century India).
D = b^2 − 4 a c is the discriminant.
Sum of roots: α + β = −b/a; product: α × β = c/a.
slides.speaker_notes: Box the formula in colour. Students should commit it to memory.

slides.title: Worked: 2 x^2 − 7 x + 3 = 0
bullets: Two roots: x = 3 and x = 1/2.
slides.speaker_notes: Have students predict the sign of D before substituting, to build the discriminant intuition.

slides.title: Discriminant — nature of the roots
bullets: D = b^2 − 4 a c.
D > 0: two distinct real roots (parabola crosses x-axis twice).
D = 0: one repeated real root x = −b/(2a) (parabola touches x-axis).
D < 0: no real roots (parabola does not meet the x-axis).
If a, b, c are rational, real roots are rational iff D is a perfect square.
slides.speaker_notes: Sketch the three parabola pictures on the board next to the bullets. The visual is what students remember a year later.

slides.title: Discriminant in action
bullets: 3 x^2 − 5 x + 2 = 0: D = 1 → two distinct rational roots.
x^2 − 4 x + 4 = 0: D = 0 → repeated root x = 2.
x^2 + x + 1 = 0: D = −3 → no real roots.
k x^2 − 4 x + 1 = 0 has equal roots when D = 0, i.e. k = 4.
For k = 4 the repeated root is x = 1/2.
slides.speaker_notes: Last two bullets: solving for a missing parameter. Common board exam question type.

slides.title: Word problems — four-step recipe
bullets: Step 1: name the unknown (usually x).
Step 2: translate the conditions into a quadratic equation.
Step 3: solve by any of the three methods.
Step 4: reject roots that contradict the situation (negative length, age, speed).
Always sanity-check the surviving root in the original problem.
slides.speaker_notes: Stress step 4 — failing to discard a negative dimension is the most common error in board exams.

slides.title: Word problem — train speed
bullets: A train covers 360 km. With speed 5 km/h more, time would be 1 h less.
Simplify: x^2 + 5 x − 1800 = 0.
Original speed = 40 km/h (reject the negative root).
slides.speaker_notes: Walk through the algebraic simplification carefully — most slips happen at the 'multiply through by x(x+5)' step.

slides.title: You try (5 minutes)
bullets: 1. Solve x^2 − 5 x + 6 = 0 by factorisation.
2. Solve x^2 − 4 x + 1 = 0 by the quadratic formula.
3. State the nature of roots of 4 x^2 − 12 x + 9 = 0.
4. The product of two consecutive positive integers is 156. Find them.
Compare answers with your bench partner.
slides.speaker_notes: Walk the room. Watch for sign errors and for students forgetting the ± in the formula.

slides.title: Quick check
bullets: Q1. Write 3 x − x^2 + 4 = 0 in standard form a x^2 + b x + c = 0.
Q2. What is the discriminant of x^2 + 2 x + 5?
Q3. If α + β = 6 and α β = 8, what quadratic has α, β as roots?
Q4. The roots of x^2 = 16 are: 4 only / ±4 / 16 / no real roots?
Show your answers on fingers (1 = first option …).
slides.speaker_notes: Use show-of-fingers to gauge the room. Address the question with the most disagreement.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Standard form: a x^2 + b x + c = 0, a ≠ 0; at most two real roots.
Three solving methods: factorisation, completing the square, quadratic formula.
x = (−b ± √(b^2 − 4 a c)) / (2 a) — the Sridharacharya formula.
Discriminant D = b^2 − 4 a c controls the nature of the roots (>, =, < 0).
Word problems: name the unknown, build the equation, solve, reject contradictory roots.
slides.speaker_notes: End with the 5 takeaways. Hand out the worksheet and announce the homework prompts.
